1:
Whether the opening command forbids raising a false report or receiving one is disputed by every source that touches it. Ellicott notes that the Septuagint and the Vulgate both render it receive, meaning to credit the thing and act upon it, and finds that reading suited to the clause that follows about lending a hand to false witness. Clarke reports a third rendering, publish, and refuses to choose, observing that our translators kept raise in the text and receive in the margin because the inventor and the receiver are almost equally criminal. Calvin allows either but comes down for receive, on the ground that the next words forbid putting the hand with the wicked, so that the two halves of the verse combine the better.

His reason for caring is that a lie would soon collapse of its own emptiness if nobody took it up, so that there is little difference between raising a calumny and keeping it going. Gill makes the same point from the other end, that if there were not so many ready to say report and we will report it, there would not be so many willing to invent. Henry, whom Wesley follows almost word for word here, presses the danger of the receiver and adds that we may be unable to avoid hearing a false report but must not hear it with pleasure or credit it while there is cause to doubt. He also refuses to confine the law to the courts, since a man's reputation lies as much at the mercy of any company as his life does at the mercy of a jury, with the added mischief that he cannot sue for it.

On following a multitude Henry describes the Jewish bench, where judgment went by majority and the junior voted first so that he might not be swayed by the authority of his seniors. Clarke turns it into an argument for singularity, that if there were not a crowd in the way of sin to keep one another in countenance every solitary sinner would hide his head, though he notes that the word may mean the great rather than the many, so that the warning is against deferring to rank. Keil and Delitzsch keep it judicial and render the clause as a ban on giving testimony that sides with the majority so as to pervert justice. Ellicott widens it furthest, that the words forbid being carried away by numbers in any case at all, and remarks that the maxim about the voice of the people is a favourite with many but is nowhere sanctioned in Scripture.

The third command reverses the direction of the danger, and Ellicott states the principle, that the scales must be proof equally against fear of the rich and weak compassion for the indigent, since the cause and not the person is to be weighed. Clarke reads the word for poor as the deliberate opposite of the word for great in the previous verse, and answers with the old maxim that justice be done though the heavens fall. Keil and Delitzsch use the parallel in Leviticus to overthrow Knobel's conjecture that the text should read great rather than poor, since that passage forbids partiality to either. Henry puts it bluntly, that if a poor man is a bad man it is foolish pity to let him fare the better for his poverty.
4:
Clarke reads the command about the enemy's straying ox as the seed of the Sermon on the Mount, a precept admitting no comment except the one a merciful man's life supplies. Ellicott makes the historical point sharper, that antiquity allowed an enemy no claim at all, and that even Cicero, who grants some duties toward a man who has wronged you, stops short of enjoining active kindness. Calvin turns the law inward, that a man who merely abstains from harm is not guiltless, since God reckons him a thief who lets his neighbour's property perish by negligence. He finds the extension to animals more telling still, that by requiring mercy to an enemy's beast God shows how far from vengeance he would have his children stand.

The verse about the fallen ass is obscure, and the sources handle it differently. Ellicott prefers Geddes' emendation of one letter wherever the verb occurs, yielding the plain sense that a man who would forbear to help must help notwithstanding. Calvin canvasses the interrogative reading and rejects it for the imperative, so that the command meets a man at the moment his hatred makes him want to walk on. His conclusion is that the law was framed to put enemies to work side by side over a suffering animal and so give them occasion for reconciliation, and Keil and Delitzsch reach the same practical sense, that one must not leave the owner to struggle alone.

The poor man is protected in both directions, and Gill dwells on the phrase thy poor, which binds judges to men of their own flesh committed to their charge under the God who protects the fatherless. Ellicott states the symmetry, that if poverty is no ground for favour it is less a ground for disfavour, and Clarke that a judge must neither countenance the poor in their crimes nor condemn them in their righteousness. Calvin anticipates the objection that judges rarely err on the poor man's side, answering that ambition can make a man generous at another's expense, a temptation the more dangerous because the injustice wears the cloak of virtue. He adds that poor litigants are often the more obstinate, and when their case fails have recourse to tears which deceive judges who think a rich man can afford to lose.

On keeping far from a false matter Ellicott takes the offence to be a false accusation, which may end in a man's death and make the accuser a murderer. Calvin considers whether the verse belongs under the sixth commandment rather than the ninth, and keeps it where it is, since the false witness kills his brother with his tongue more surely than the executioner with his sword. Keil and Delitzsch call the thing judicial murder and note the threat attached. Wesley reads that threat as a promise turned round, that God will condemn the man who unjustly condemns others.

Against bribes Clarke reaches for Magna Charta and its article that to none will we sell, to none deny or defer, right or justice, recalling how the largest present to the crown once decided a suit. Ellicott adds that Josephus reports a bribed judge was punished with death, and yet the prophets show Hebrew judges no better than any others, corrupt justice being among the evils that brought on the captivity. Calvin puts it most forcibly, that a tribunal is a sanctuary for the oppressed and nothing is uglier than for them to fall among robbers there, since gifts infect a sound mind before they soil the hand. On the stranger Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the reason given, that Israel knew from the inside what a stranger's heart feels, while Ellicott reads the law's repetition as evidence of how strongly they were inclined to ill-use him.
10:
Henry gives three purposes for the year of rest, to show what a plentiful land could feed so many without foreign trade, to remind Israel that their landlord was God and to try their obedience where it touched their interest, and to teach the same trust in providence that the sixth day's manna had taught. Clarke sets out Calmet's five, which add the levelling of condition among the people and the detaching of their affections from perishable things. Gill puts the first of these more sharply, that the law declared God the true proprietor and Israel his tenants, while giving the land itself a rest that made it more fruitful afterwards. Ellicott notes how far the levelling went, since the owner took no larger share of that year's produce than the hireling, the stranger or the cattle, and the vineyards and oliveyards would still bear a full crop.

Clarke works out the arithmetic of the promise in Leviticus, that the sixth year would yield not three harvests but one equal to three, since it had to carry the sixth, the seventh and the eighth, a whole round of seasons being needed before the eighth year's sowing could be eaten. He then makes the observation that troubles him most, that the keeping of this ordinance is nowhere expressly recorded in Scripture, and infers that the people could not trust God so far, until the captivity gave the land the sabbaths their unbelief had denied it. He adds that commentators cannot agree when the year began, since starting it in spring would cost two harvests while starting it in autumn would not. Keil and Delitzsch place both this law and the sabbath among the duties men owe each other rather than among the feasts that follow, on the ground that in both the care of the poor stands in the foreground.

That the weekly sabbath is repeated here Henry takes as a guard against supposing that in a year of rest the seventh day might be laid in common with the rest. Ellicott reads the juxtaposition as deliberate, marking the two as parts of one system which culminated in the jubilee, and observes that nothing is added to the fourth commandment except a fuller statement of its mercy. Clarke presses that mercy toward the animals, asking whether God cares for oxen and answering that he does, with a complaint that English cattle are worked to death and a foreigner's saying that England is the paradise of women and the hell of horses. He also glosses the word for refreshed as re-souled, a renewal of bodily and spiritual strength together, while Calvin turns the same clause on the masters, that men who had themselves been slaves in Egypt could judge from their own feelings how intolerable cruelty is.

On making no mention of other gods Ellicott reports the Jewish and Vulgate reading, that swearing by them is what is forbidden, and holds the words reach much further, to ignoring the names altogether. He then qualifies his own rule honestly, allowing the preacher's warning and the historian's necessity, and noting that Moses himself names Baal, Chemosh and Moloch elsewhere. Calvin ties the verse to the third commandment instead, since a man who swears by another god transfers to it the honour of being the knower of hearts and the judge of souls. Henry, whom Wesley again follows word for word, takes the opening clause as a caution over the whole chapter, that a man may ruin himself by mere carelessness but cannot save himself without great circumspection, and wishes the names of the heathen deities were less familiar in Christian schools.
14:
Gill and Clarke name the three feasts and what each commemorated, the deliverance from Egypt, the giving of the law, and the forty years in tents, Clarke adding Calmet's account of why God appointed festivals at all and a long list of the lesser Jewish feasts. Calvin finds it strange that only three appearances are required when Moses elsewhere enumerates more, and asks pointedly where the feast of trumpets and the day of atonement have gone. His answer is partly that the principal feasts alone are named, and partly that the three holy days of the seventh month fell so close together that one journey covered them all, named after the most remarkable, since keeping every family in Jerusalem a whole month would have been a burden. He draws from that a rule about worship generally, that God prescribed only three necessary convocations because he approves no service which does not proceed from a cheerful heart, and Wesley notes the three fall in spring, summer and autumn, avoiding both winter travel and the height of harvest.

Who was obliged to come is defined narrowly by all who touch it. Keil and Delitzsch restrict the command to males, probably those above twenty who had been numbered, while insisting that women and boys were not thereby shut out. Gill preserves the Mishnaic list of the exempt, which runs from the deaf and the blind to the aged and whoever cannot walk, and Clarke reports the rabbinic limits of age at either end. Wesley infers a further exemption from the rule that nobody was to appear empty, since servants would mostly have had nothing to bring, and Ellicott turns that same rule on the reader, that thanksgiving owes God something more substantial than the calves of our lips.

Ellicott supplies the practical detail of the later observance, that Pentecost fell fifty days after the harvest began and opened with two loaves of the new wheat, and that although the law fixed it to one day it was early extended to two in case the reckoning had slipped. He describes the ingathering as something like a harvest-home but longer and more religious, held when vintage and olive-harvest were over, with the booths recalling the wilderness. On the rule about leaven, Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke agree the sacrifice meant is the paschal lamb, called God's sacrifice by eminence, and that the prohibition holds as long as any leaven remains in the house. Ellicott notes that some would extend it to every sacrifice but the majority do not, since leavened bread was actually commanded at Pentecost, and prefers to read the second clause as the fat of my feast rather than of my sacrifice.

The kid boiled in its mother's milk divides them four ways. Clarke reports Cudworth's Karaite manuscript, that the heathen boiled a kid in its dam's milk and sprinkled the liquid over their fields by magic to make them fruitful, a custom Spenser traced among the Zabii, and Wesley repeats it while wondering whether cruelty is not the better reason. Ellicott calls the magical explanation fanciful and refutes it from Deuteronomy, where the precept stands among unclean meats and so concerns a kid boiled to be eaten, preferring Bochart's account that the cruelty lies in making the milk meant to feed the creature the means of cooking it. Calvin will have none of the dietary reading at all, arguing from the threefold repetition and from the company each occurrence keeps that the rule belongs to the sacrifices, and that God would not admit so monstrous a thing as flesh seethed in what was almost its own blood, while Clarke ends where the others converge, that the precept forbids whatever would blunt the moral feelings.
20:
Who the promised Angel is occupies every source in the chapter. Gill reports the rabbinic guesses, the book of the law, the ark, Michael, or the Metatron whose name Jarchi says is as his master's, and notes that some ancient Jews made him the Redeemer of the world. Henry sets the two Christian options side by side without choosing, a created minister of providence or the Son of God, since we may as well suppose him the church's Redeemer before his incarnation as the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. Clarke rejects Moses and Joshua and calls in Philo, who describes God's own Word as viceroy over the sacred flock and quotes this very verse, a testimony he values because its author was no Christian.

Calvin argues at length against the rabbis who make the Angel Joshua, objecting that Israel would then have had no leader through the desert. He rests the positive case on Paul, who warns the Corinthians not to tempt Christ as their fathers did in the wilderness. The decisive phrase for him is that God's name is in the Angel, passed over too lightly by others, since it grants him the knowledge of hearts and the power of judgment Scripture reserves to God alone. He also catches a play on words, the same verb serving for the Angel keeping Israel and for Israel keeping itself. Ellicott makes the shortest argument of all, that God is never said to set his Name in a man, while Keil and Delitzsch put the phrase simply, that Jehovah revealed himself in this Angel, and Wesley glosses the Name as his nature and his authority.

Henry turns to the terms, that Christ saves only those who obey him, and that a people whose defence may depart do well not to provoke their protector. He reads the promise against their enemies as a league offensive and defensive, like the one made with Abraham, so that God twists his interests together with his people's. Calvin sees the softening as deliberate, that God moderates the terror he has raised lest anxiety deaden their sense of his mercy, and points to the roll of nations they could never have matched alone. Clarke notices that six nations are named here where the Septuagint adds the Girgashite, and Ellicott qualifies the threat, that to cut them off means to end them as nations rather than exterminate them, since Jebusites and Hittites survived.

On the images Ellicott makes a distinction the others do not, that the Canaanites were driven out for profligacy rather than idolatry, and notes that Israel was forbidden the conqueror's usual practice of keeping idols as trophies. Calvin separates permanent from temporary in the same command, the condemnation of superstition standing to the end of the world while the order to demolish was an enactment for that time. He draws the consequence for his own day without hesitation, that Christians may keep buildings once polluted by idols and put them to better use. From the words about coming into the land to possess it he follows Augustine in inferring that no private man is commissioned to destroy idols, the authority belonging to a people once they hold the country.

The closing promises are read plainly by all. Henry counts four, food, health, increase and length of days, and observes that God's blessing makes bread and water more nourishing than a feast of fat things without it. Ellicott suggests half the sicknesses men suffer are the fruit of their own living, and notes that the ancient world read barrenness and untimely births as marks of divine displeasure. Calvin observes what the list leaves out, that in so fertile a land no wine or oil is named but only bread and water, as though God undertook for the necessary supports of life and no more.
27:
Gill offers two accounts of the fear sent before Israel, either the hornets of the next verse or the reputation of what God had done in Egypt and at the Red Sea, which made the inhabitants melt. Calvin insists on something inward, that God depresses men's hearts by secret inspiration, so that courage and cowardice alike are in his hand where the heathen can only speak of fortune. He cites Rahab as a witness who went halfway, tracing her people's melting hearts to a sense of God's power without saying they were struck from heaven, and observes that Moses ascends higher. Wesley puts it in a sentence, that they who fear will soon flee, and that God can chastise his people's enemies by such mean creatures.

Whether the hornets are insects at all divides the sources evenly. Gill and Clarke take them literally, Gill citing Aelian on the Phaselites driven from their country by wasps and Clarke arguing from the creature's ferocity that a few thousand would rout the best army. Clarke supports this from his own failure to hold a hornet in a pair of forceps, and from Joshua's word that two Amorite kings were driven out this way without sword or bow. Keil and Delitzsch know the same precedents and refuse the conclusion, since Joshua records no such extermination, and Ellicott proposes that the hornets are the Egyptians, whose armies broke the Hittite power while Israel was in the desert, and whose hieroglyph for king was a bee.

Gill reports a further possibility, that the word means a wasting disease, which Aben Ezra took for something like leprosy. Calvin declines the natural question and takes the point to be the smallness of the instrument, that God promised not great warriors but insects, to show he would arm the least of his creatures. On the slowness of the conquest he finds a mercy, that a land emptied at once would have been overrun by beasts more troublesome than the men, and Gill draws the parallel that corruption is left in the converted for the exercise of their graces. Ellicott confirms the danger historically, that exactly this happened when Assyria deported the Samaritans and lions multiplied in the empty land.

Calvin adds the sting, that Israel's long mixture with the nations was their own fault, their slackness fulfilling Joshua's warning that the remnant would be snares and thorns. On the promised bounds Clarke and Ellicott agree the description was fulfilled under Solomon and not before, Ellicott adding that the River can mean nothing but the Euphrates, and Clarke that God's promises are fulfilled to few because men are slow to believe. Calvin follows the promise further, through David as a prototype to Zechariah's word of a final restoration, and concludes it was accomplished only when Christ took in the four quarters of the globe. Had the Jews continued faithful, he adds, the Gentiles would have been joined to them, whereas their rebellion left a place empty which the Gentiles filled.

The ban on covenants Ellicott explains from the diplomacy of the age, since treaties regularly acknowledged each other's gods, so that a treaty with a people was a treaty with its deities. He allows that individuals might remain as proselytes and the Gibeonites in servitude, so that what was forbidden was an independent heathen community beside Israel. Gill extends the prohibition to marriage, which Israel contracted notwithstanding and found a snare, and Clarke grounds the severity in Israel's office of keeping true religion until the Messiah came. Clarke closes by turning on the reader, regretting how little the law of Moses is studied for its justice and humanity, and urging that whoever loves his enemy and obeys Christ's voice finds the road plain before him.
